docs.title: Hands on Labs - CDF
docs.text:
Welcome to the Cloudera DataFlow Hands-on Labs! These labs will equip you with practical skills for building, testing, and deploying real-time data pipelines on Cloudera Data Platform.

You will learn how to design and deploy NiFi flows with the CDF Flow Designer, manage schemas with Schema Registry, stream data into Apache Kafka, run real-time analytics with SQL Stream Builder (Flink), persist results in Apache Kudu, and capture database changes end-to-end using Kafka Connect with Debezium CDC.

Please select your user below — your selection will persist throughout all labs in this browser session and automatically populate your username and database information in all code examples.

Select User -- Select -- user001 user002 user003 user004 user005 user006 user007 user008 user009 user010 user011 user012 user013 user014 user015 user016 user017 user018 user019 user020 SELECT USER ✕ Active user: None

  • Lab 0. Prerequisite Setup

    Goals

    • Configure your workload password for authenticating to data services in upcoming labs
    • Understand the purpose of the workload password in CDP

    Go to Lab 0 Guide

  • Lab 1. Data Distribution with CDF

    Goals

    • Learn to use Flow Designer for low-code data flow development
    • Test and version-control flows in DataFlow Catalog
    • Practice flow design best practices

    Go to Lab 1 Guide

  • Lab 2. Streaming Analytics with Stream Processing

    Goals

    • Set up Change Data Capture (CDC) using Kafka Connect
    • Configure source and sink connectors for CDC
    • Monitor CDC pipeline and validate data movement
    • Troubleshoot common CDC issues

    Go to Lab 2 Guide

  • Lab 3. CDC with Kafka Connect

    Goals

    • Explore advanced CDC scenarios with Kafka Connect
    • Tune connector configurations for performance
    • Handle schema evolution and data transformations
    • Integrate CDC pipelines with downstream analytics

    Go to Lab 3 Guide

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
This first step is designed to prepare your user and ensure you have the necessary credentials to access the data services in the upcoming labs:

  • Access the Cloudera Control Plane
  • Set your Workload Password for authenticating to data services in upcoming labs

docs.title: Configure Your Workload Password
docs.text:
From the home screen, click your username (top right) and select “Profile” from the drop-down menu. From the new page, click the “Set Workload Password” hyperlink.

Step 1. Top right corner on CDP home screen.

Step 2. Click on "Set Workload Password"

What is the workdload password?

Nifi and SQL Stream Builder needs the workload password for :

In the Cloudera Data Platform (CDP) Public Cloud, the workload password (often referred to as the FreeIPA password) is a secondary set of credentials used specifically to authenticate with the actual clusters and data services running in your environment.

Step 3. Enter your new workload password and confirm it.

After setting your workload password, make sure to remember it as you will need it to authenticate to the services in the upcoming labs. You can change this password at any time from your profile settings.

docs.title: Lab 1 - Data Distribution with Cloudera DataFlow
Overview
docs.text:
In this module you will practice creating, testing and deploying a flow in Cloudera DataFlow service. You will learn to:

  • Develop flows using the low-code Flow Designer.
  • Create a test session and interactively test a flow.
  • Version-control a flow into the DataFlow Catalog.
  • Deploy a flow on an auto-scaling production cluster on k8s.
  • Use Stream Messaging Manager to inspect Kafka topics.

docs.title: 2. Design the flow in the Flow Designer
2.1 Create a new flow

docs.title: 2.2 Configure parameters for the flow

The default context is automatically bound to every Process Group in your flow, making all parameters available throughout.

docs.title: 2.3 Create Controller Services
docs.text:
About Controller Services

Controller Services are shared configuration points that provide settings for use by processors and other services. Rather than configuring the same information in every processor, a Controller Service defines it once and makes it available to any component that needs it.

  1. Enable the Test Session before configuring the services
    • Select Flow Options > Test Session. Use the latest NiFi version (default).
    • Click Start Test Session. Test session status changes to Initializing Test Session…
    • Wait for the status to change to Active Test Session.

You are not yet at the point of testing the flow, but enabling a test session forces the Default NiFi SSL Context Service controller service to be created, which you will need in the next steps.

  1. Click Flow Options > Services

  2. Add a new ClouderaSchemaRegistry controller service

  • In the text box, filter for ClouderaSchemaRegistry, select it and click Add.
  • For service name, enter WS_CDP_Schema_Registry
  • Click Add Service. The Add Service page opens.

docs.title: Configure the ClouderaSchemaRegistry service:
docs.text:
Property Value Service Name WS_CDP_Schema_Registry Schema Registry URL #{Schema Registry URL} SSL Context Service Default NiFi SSL Context Service Basic Authentication Username #{CDP Workload User} Basic Authentication Password #{CDP Workload User Password}
  • Click Apply, activate the service by clicking on the Enable icon

  1. Add a new Syslog5424Reader controller service - Click Add Service. The Add Service page opens. - In the text box, filter for Syslog5424Reader, select it and click Add - Configure the Syslog5424Reader service:

    Property Value Service Name WS_Syslog_5424_Reader
  • Click Apply, activate the service by clicking on the Enable icon

  1. Add a new JsonTreeReader controller service - Click Add Service. The Add Service page opens. - In the text box, filter for JsonTreeReader, select it and click Add - Configure the JsonTreeReader service:

    Property Value Service Name WS_JSON_Syslog_Reader Schema Access Strategy Use 'Schema Name' Property Schema Registry WS_CDP_Schema_Registry Schema Name #{Schema Name}
  • Click Apply, activate the service by clicking on the Enable icon

  1. Add a new JsonRecordSetWriter controller service - Click Add Service. The Add Service page opens. - In the text box, filter for JsonRecordSetWriter, select it and click Add - Configure the JsonRecordSetWriter service:

    Property Value Service Name WS_JSON_Syslog_Writer Schema Write Strategy Set 'schema.name' Attribute Schema Access Strategy Use 'Schema Name' Property Schema Registry WS_CDP_Schema_Registry Schema Name #{Schema Name}
  • Click Apply, activate the service by clicking on the Enable icon

  1. Add a new AvroRecordSetWriter controller service - Click Add Service. The Add Service page opens. - In the text box, filter for AvroRecordSetWriter, select it and click Add - Configure the AvroRecordSetWriter service:

    Property Value Service Name WS_Avro_Syslog_Writer Schema Write Strategy Embed Avro Schema Schema Access Strategy Use 'Schema Name' Property Schema Registry WS_CDP_Schema_Registry Schema Name #{Schema Name}
  • Click Apply, activate the service by clicking on the Enable icon

docs.title: 2.4 Design the flow
docs.text: Open the Flow Design page

docs.title: 2.4.1 Add the Generate Syslog RFC5424 Processor
docs.text:
1. Drag the Processor icon onto the canvas
  2. Select the ExecuteScript processor.
  3. Configure the processor as follows:
  4. Processor Name: Generate Syslog RFC5424
  5. Concurrent Tasks: 4
  6. Run Schedule: 1 sec

  7. Execution: Primary Node

  8. Properties:

    1. Script Engine: python
    2. Script Body: copy and paste the following script:
##
## Author: Nasheb Ismaily
## Description: Generates a random RFC5424 format syslog message
##
from org.apache.commons.io import IOUtils
from java.nio.charset import StandardCharsets
from org.apache.nifi.processor.io import OutputStreamCallback
import random
from datetime import datetime

class PyOutputStreamCallback(OutputStreamCallback):
    def __init__(self):
        pass
    def process(self, outputStream):
        hostname = "host"
        domain_name = ".example.com"
        tag = ["kernel", "python", "application"]
        version = "1"
        nouns = "application"
        verbs = ("started", "stopped", "exited", "completed")
        adv = ("successfully", "unexpectedly", "cleanly", "gracefully")
        for i in range(1,10):
            application = "{0}{1}".format(nouns, random.choice(range(1, 11)))
            message_id = "ID{0}".format(random.choice(range(1, 50)))
            random_tag = random.choice(tag)
            structured_data = "[SDID iut=\"{0}\" eventSource=\"{1}\" eventId=\"{2}\"]".format(random.choice(range(1, 10)), random_tag, random.choice(range(1, 100)))
            time_output = datetime.utcnow().strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%f')[:-3] + 'Z'
            random_host = random.choice(range(1, 11))
            fqdn = "{0}{1}{2}".format(hostname, random_host, domain_name)
            random_pid = random.choice(range(500, 9999))
            priority = random.choice(range(0, 191))
            num = random.randrange(0, 4)
            random_message = application + ' has ' + verbs[num] + ' ' + adv[num]
            syslog_output = ("<{0}>{1} {2} {3} {4} {5} {6} {7} {8}\n".format(priority, version, time_output, fqdn, application,random_pid, message_id,structured_data, random_message))
            outputStream.write(bytearray(syslog_output.encode('utf-8')))

flowFile = session.create()
if (flowFile != None):
    flowFile = session.write(flowFile, PyOutputStreamCallback())
    session.transfer(flowFile, REL_SUCCESS)
  1. Relationships: check Terminate for the failure relationship

  1. Click Apply

There should be now four processors on the canvas, as shown in the diagram below:

docs.title: 2.4.5 Connect the Processors
docs.text:
Connect the processors as shown in the diagram below:

  • Connect Generate Syslog RFC5424 → Filter Events for relationship success
  • Connect Filter Events → Write To Kafka - Avro for relationship filtered_event
  • Connect Filter Events → Write To Kafka - JSON for relationship filtered_event
  • Connect Write To Kafka → itself to retry for failures

docs.title: 2.5 Naming the queues
docs.text:
Providing unique names to all queues is important when creating flows in CDP-PC. The queue names are used to define Key Performance Indicators and having unique names for them make it easier to understand and create CDF-PC dashboards.

To name a queue, double-click the queue and give it a unique name. The best practice here is to start with the existing queue name (i.e. success, failure, retry, etc…) and, if that name is not unique, add the source and destination processor to the name.

For example:

  • The success queue between Generate Flow File and Filter Events should be named success_generate-Filter-Events
  • The success queue between Filter Events and Write To Kafka should be named filtered_event_Filter-WriteToKafka

  • The failure retry queue from Write To Kafka to itself should be named failure_WriteToKafka

docs.title: 3. Interactively test the flow
docs.text:
Test sessions are a feature in the CDF Flow Designer that allow you to start/stop processors and work with live data to validate your data flow logic.

To test your draft flow, start a Test Session by clicking Flow Options > Test Session > Start Test Session. This launches a NiFi sandbox to enable you to validate your draft flow and interactively work with live data by starting and stopping components.

If your session is already started, right click on the blank canvas and press Enable and then right click again and select Start to start the flow. You can also start individual processors by right clicking on them and selecting Start.

Note

If you had previously started and stopped a test session, the Start button is replaced with the Restart button. Clicking on Restart restarts the session with the same settings used previously. If you want to change the settings, click on the Edit Settings button.

  1. If your test session is not yet started, start one by clicking on Flow Options > Test Session > Start.

  2. Click Start Test Session (accept all defaults). Test session status changes to Initializing Test Session…

  3. Wait for the status to change to Active Test Session.

  4. Click Flow Options > Services to enable Controller Services, if not already enabled.

  5. Start all processors in case they are not running.

  • The flow starts executing. On the Flow Design Canvas you can observe statistics on your processors change as they consume data and execute their respective tasks.

docs.title: 4. Publishing the Flow
docs.text:
When your flow draft has been tested and is ready to be used, you can publish it to the DataFlow Catalog and deploy it from there. The first time a flow is published, you will be asked to provide a unique name that does not already exist in the catalog.

Flow Versioning

After a flow is published, subsequent changes will be saved as new versions in the catalog under the same name. This name cannot be changed.

When you want to publish a draft flow as a flow definition, you have two options:

Option1

  • On the Flow Design Canvas, click Flow Options > Publish To Catalog > Publish Flow.

Option2

  • Click on Flow Design (left-hand side) to see the All Flows page, which lists all the flows. Then click on the menu for the flow you want to publish and select View Flow Workspace.

This will take you to the list of all flows running on the same environment (workspace) as the flow you selected. To publish the flow, Workspace view, click again on the menu for the desired flow and select Publish Flow.

  1. Choose one of the methods explained above and publish your flow.
  2. In the Publish Flow dialog box, enter the following details:
  3. Flow Name: USERNAME-syslog-kafka-flow
  4. Collection: Select Unassigned
  5. Click Publish.

docs.title: 5. Deploy the flow in Production
docs.text:
After the flow is published it will be saved in the DataFlow Catalog and you can deploy it from there. Right after publishing the flow, there will be a modal popout to deploy the flow. You can deploy it from there.

Optionally, you can deploy the flow from the DataFlow Catalog. To do that, follow these steps:

  1. Search for the flow in the Flow Catalog
  2. Click on the Flow to see its details:

docs.text:
1. Click on the Deploy button to deploy the flow, select Create New Deployment

  2. Select the CDP environment where this flow will be deployed and click Continue

3. Give the deployment a unique name ( USERNAME-syslog-kafka-flow), then click Next

  1. In the NiFi Configuration page correct defaults are already pre-selected, click Next.

  2. In the Parameters page, all other values are pre-filled. However, you must re-enter the CDP Workload User Password.

Parameter Value CDP Workload Password The workload password for the current user
  1. In the Sizing & Scaling page update the following and then click Next
Setting Value Size Extra Small (PRE-SELECTED) Enable Auto Scaling True Min Nodes 1 (PRE-SELECTED) Max Nodes 3

  1. In the Key Performance Indicators page, click on Add New KPI to add the following KPIs.

  2. Add KPI 1:

Setting Value KPI Scope Connection Connection Name failure_WriteToKafka Metrics to Track Bytes Queued Trigger alert when metric is greater than 1 MB Alert triggered when outside boundary for 30 seconds

  1. Add KPI 2:
Setting Value KPI Scope Connection Connection Name filtered_event_Filter-WriteToKafka Metrics to Track Bytes Queued Trigger alert when metric is greater than 10 KB Alert triggered when outside boundary for 30 seconds

  2. Click Deploy to initiate the flow deployment, deployment will take a few minutes to complete. Following screen will be shown while the deployment is in progress.

docs.title: 6. Inspect Kafka topics in Stream Messaging Manager (SMM)
docs.text:
Use SMM to to show the kafka topics USERNAME-syslog-avro and USERNAME-syslog-json that is being written to from the NiFi flow.

  3. Click on the Topics tab to see the list of topics in the Kafka cluster.

  4. Inside the SMM, filter the topics under USERNAME, which were created by the NiFi flow in Module 1

  5. Click on the Profile icon for the topic USERNAME-syslog-avro, as shown below:

  6. On the Topic page, click on the Data Explorer tab:

  7. Change the Value Deserializer to Avro to use the Schema Registry integration and verify that the data was deserialized correctly:

  8. Open the USERNAME-syslog-json topic and verify inside the Data Explorer tab that the data is in JSON format and can be viewed directly in the SMM UI.

We have now concluded Lab 1

docs.title: Lab 2 - Streaming Analytics with Stream Processing
Streaming Analytics with Cloudera Stream Processing
Overview
docs.text:
In this module you will practice the streaming analytic capabilities of Cloudera Stream Processing service using SQL Stream Builder to develop and deploy a real-time streaming job in production.

  • Create a Project in SQL Stream Builder (SSB).
  • Register Schema Registry and Kudu Catalogs in SSB.
  • Create Virtual Tables in SSB.
  • Create and execute Jobs in SSB.

docs.title: 1. Configure SSB Project
docs.text:
We will use this URL to configure the SSB project in the next steps.

  1. In the CDP Console, find the Streaming Analytics (Flink) DataHub and click on it to open the DataHub page.

  2. In the Projects page, click on the New Project button:

  3. Enter the following details in the Create Project dialog box:

Field Value Name USERNAME-project

  1. The new project will be listed in the Projects page:

docs.title: 3. Register a Kafka Data Source
docs.text:
Before you can use SSB to process data from Kafka topics you must register one or more Kafka clusters as Data Sources in your project. In this section you will register the Kafka DataHub as your data source.

  1. In your project workspace, expand the Data Sources item in the navigation tree. You will see two items under it: "Kafka" and "Catalog"

  2. Click on the 3 dot menu of the Kafka node to create a new Kafka data source:

  3. Provide the following details in the Kafka Data Source dialog box:

Field Value Name USERNAME-dh-kafka Brokers <broker1>:9093,<broker2>:9093,<broker3>:9093 (see screenshot below for the instruction) Protocol SASL/SSL SASL Mechanism PLAIN SASL Username USERNAME SASL Password <your workload password>

For Kafka Brokers find the SMM Datahub, click on the Endpoints tab and copy the brokers, as shown in the screenshot below. Use that to fill in the Brokers field in the Kafka Data Source dialog box.

After all the fields are filled in, click on the Validate link to validate the data source. If the data source is successfully validated you will see a message saying "Data Source is valid".

Once data source is validated, click on the Create button to register the Kafka data source. You will see it listed under the Kafka node in the navigation tree.

docs.title: 4. Register a Schema Registry catalog
docs.text:
Schema Registry stores schemas that are used to read/write data from/to Kafka topics. Registering a Schema Registry instance in SSB automatically creates SSB tables for the schemas retrieved from it, making it simpler to start accessing data from those topics.

  1. In your project workspace, navigate to Data Sources -> Catalog. Click the 3 dot menu of the Catalog item and select New Catalog to create a new catalog.

  1. Select Schema Registry Catalog Type, enter the following details in the Catalog dialog box:

For getting the Schema Hostname, find the SMM Datahub, click on the Nodes tab and copy the master node hostname, as shown in the screenshot below. Use that to fill in the Schema Registry URL field in the Catalog dialog box.

Field Value Name USERNAME-dh-schreg Kafka Cluster USERNAME-dh-kafka Enable TLS Enabled Schema Registry URL https://<schreg_hostname>:7790/api/v1 (Find the Schema Hostname in the SMM Datahub under the Nodes tab)

  1. Click on the Validate link to validate the Catalog. If the catalog is successfully validated you will see a message saying "Data Source is valid". If you hover the mouse over that message you will see how many tables were discovered from Schema Registry during the validation:

  2. Once the catalog is validated. Press the Create button to register the Schema Registry catalog.

docs.title: 5. Register a Kudu catalog
docs.text:
Similar to a Schema Registry catalog, a Kudu catalog makes Kudu tables automatically available for use in SSB, simplifying the process of mapping Virtual Tables to the actual Kudu ones. In this section you will register the DataHub Kudu cluster as a catalog in your SSB project.

This will make the syslog_severity table, which has already been created in Kudu, available for queries in SSB.

  1. In your project workspace, navigate to Data Sources -> Catalog. Click the kebab menu of the Catalog item and select New Catalog to create a new catalog.

  2. Enter the following details in the Catalog dialog box:

Field Value Name USERNAME-dh-kudu Catalog Type Kudu Kudu Masters <kudu_master1>:7051,<kudu_master2>:7051,<kudu_master3>:7051

Note

Kudu Masters: The hostname of the Kudu master nodes can be found in the Real-time Data Mart (Kudu) DataHub page. In the CDP Console, find your Real-time Data Mart DataHub and click on the Nodes tab. Copy the FQDN for the 3 masters, as shown in the screenshot below.

The full masters address to be provided during the catalog registration is the following:

  1. Click on the Validate link to validate the Catalog. If the catalog is successfully validated you will see a message saying "Data Source is valid". Hover over that message — it will show how many tables were discovered. You should see at least 1 table (the syslog_severity table). If it shows 0 tables, the Kudu Masters address is incorrect — go back and verify the FQDNs from the DataHub Nodes tab.

  2. Once the catalog is validated, press the Create button to register the Kudu catalog.

  3. After registration, expand External Resources → Virtual Tables → USERNAME-dh-kudu in the left navigation tree. You will see the database and table names exactly as SSB exposes them. Note the exact full path (catalog → database → table) — you will need this precise path in your SQL queries.

Do this step before proceeding to section 7.4

You must know the exact table path before writing the job4 query. Use CTRL+SPACE auto-complete in the SQL editor to find and insert the correct fully-qualified table name.

After registering all data sources in your SSB project, you should see them listed under the Data Sources node in the navigation tree:

docs.title: 6. Create a Kafka Table manually
docs.text:
You saw that registering a Schema Registry catalog automatically exposes all discovered schemas as SSB Virtual Tables, simplifying access to the corresponding Kafka topics.

In cases where a topic has no associated schema, SSB allows you to define a Virtual Table manually — specifying the schema and the Kafka topic mapping directly. The steps below walk through this process using the New Kafka Table wizard.

How schema inference works SSB can inspect the data flowing through a JSON topic and automatically infer the schema — useful when no formal schema exists. However, there must be data in the topic already for this feature to work correctly. Schema inference is best-effort. Data types may occasionally be inferred incorrectly, so always review the inferred schema and adjust as needed before proceeding.

  1. In your project workspace, navigate to Data Sources -> Virtual Tables.

  2. Click the kebab menu of the Virtual Tables item and select New Kafka Table to create a new virtual table.

  1. Enter the following details in the Kafka Table dialog box:
Field Value Table Name syslog_data Kafka Cluster USERNAME-dh-kafka Data Format JSON Topic Name USERNAME-syslog-json
  1. Click on Detect Schema to infer the schema automatically.

  1. You will also notice that a "Schema is invalid" message appears upon the schema detection. If you hover the mouse over the message it shows the reason:

  1. Each record read from Kafka by SSB has an associated timestamp column of data type TIMESTAMP ROWTIME. By default, this timestamp is sourced from the internal timestamp of the Kafka message and is exposed through a column called eventTimestamp.

However, if your message payload already contains a timestamp associated with the event (event time), you may want to use that instead of the Kafka internal timestamp.

In this case, the syslog message has a field called "timestamp" that contains the timestamp you should use. You want to expose this field as the table's "event_time" column. To do this, click on the Event Time tab and enter the following properties:

Property Value Input Timestamp Column timestamp Event Time Column event_time Watermark Seconds 3 Use Kafka Timestamps Disable

  1. Now that you have configured the event time column, click on Detect Schema again. You should see the schema turn valid.

8. Click the Create and Review button to create the table.

  1. Review the table's DDL and click Close.

docs.title: 7. Create Streaming SQL jobs
docs.text:
In this section you will practice creating and executing SQL Streaming jobs to implement different types of use cases. You will create the following jobs:

  • Job 1: Selecting records from a Kafka virtual table
  • Job 2: Selecting records from a Schema Registry virtual table
  • Job 3: Using a windowing function
  • Job 4: Enriching streaming data with data-at-rest data sources

docs.title: 7.1. Job 1: Selecting records from a Kafka virtual table
docs.text:
1. In the SSB console, ensure you have switched to your project and you are at your project's main page.
  2. On the Explorer view, click the 3 dot menu of the Jobs item and select New Job to create a new one.
  1. Enter job1 as a Job Name and click on the Create button:
  1. Click on the SQL editor area and type the job query.

In this first job you will simply select everything from the syslog_data table that you created previously. Notice that the editor has auto-completion for keywords, table names, etc. As you type you will see suggestions for completion being shown. To select one of the options, simply use the arrow keys to scroll to the option and press \<ENTER>.

If the list of options doesn't not show at a particular position of the cursor you can press \<CTRL>+\<SPACE> to show the list of completion suggestions.

  1. In the editor type "SELECT * FROM " (with a space in the end) and then press \<CTRL>+\<SPACE>. Select the syslog_data table from the list.

  1. Click Execute.

The Logs tab will show that the job execution has started and once data is retrieved it will automatically switch to the Results tab to show the results:

  1. You will notice that the Results tab shows approximately one record every second, even though there is a lot more data flowing through the Kafka topic. This is because, by default, SSB only shows a sample of the data on the screen to give the user some feedback about what the query is retrieving. If you leave the query running you will also notice that the sample polling will automatically stop once 100 records have been retrieved.

You can change the sample behavior and other settings by clicking on the Job Settings button, as shown below:

NOTE: Selecting "Sample all messages" can have a negative effect in performance and will increase the resource consumption of your browser as well. Use this only when necessary to check or troubleshoot data.

  1. From the Results tab you can see that the data contains records of all severities. If you want to change that you can simply stop and edit your query and run it again.

Click Stop to stop the job and edit the query so that it retrieves only records with severity 3: 

   SELECT *

   FROM syslog_data

   WHERE severity = 3

Click Execute and check the results to confirm that the change was effective.

  1. Once you're done, Stop your job. In the Explorer tree you can see all the jobs and which ones are running. You can also stop jobs from there by right-clicking on the job item. If the job status doesn't look correct, try click on the Reload icon, shown below:

docs.title: 7.2. Job 2: Selecting records from a Schema Registry virtual table
docs.text:
Once virtual tables are created in SSB, their backend and data format are transparent to the user. Tables can be queried in SSB in exactly the same way. In this section you will execute the same query from job1 against a table that comes from an Kafka topic with AVRO format and will see that everything works the same:

  1. On the Explorer view, right-click on the Jobs item and select New Job to create a new job. Call it job2.

  2. Enter the same query from the previous job, but using the USERNAME-syslog-avro table (use the auto-completion to find the correct table name - \<CTRL>+\<SPACE>). You will notice that the auto-completion will prefix the table name with the catalog and database names:

   SELECT *

   FROM **[auto-complete the table `USERNAME-syslog-avro`]**

   WHERE severity = 3

Click Execute and check the results to verify that everything works as expected.

  1. Once you're done, Stop your job.

docs.title: 7.3. Job 3: Using a windowing function
docs.text:
One powerful feature of Flink and SSB is the ability to perform windowing aggregations on streaming data. In this section you will write a query that defines a sliding (HOP) window on the syslog stream to count how many events of each severity are being generated in intervals of 30 seconds. The 30-second window slides forward every 5 seconds, so the query produces results every 5 seconds for the previous window that ended at that point in time.

  1. On the Explorer view, right-click on the Jobs item and select New Job to create a new job. Call it job3.

  2. Enter the following query in the SQL editor: 

       SELECT
     window_start, window_end,
     severity,
     count(*) as severity_count
   FROM
     TABLE(
       HOP(TABLE syslog_data,
           DESCRIPTOR(event_time),
           INTERVAL '5' SECOND,
           INTERVAL '30' SECOND))
   GROUP BY
     window_start, window_end, severity

Click Execute and check the results to verify that everything works as expected.

  1. Once you're done, Stop your job.

Tip

If you're not seeing all the counts for all the severities for each one of the aggregation windows, try setting the sample behavior to "Sample all messages".

docs.title: 7.4. Job 4: Enriching streaming data with data-at-rest data sources
docs.text:
Another powerful feature of Flink/SSB is that you can write queries joining tables that have different backends. A Kafka streaming table, for example, can be joined with batch tables stored in relational databases, Kudu or even HDFS.

This opens a number of possibilities like using data-at-rest tables to enrich streaming data. In this section you will create a job that enriches the aggregation stream produced by the query from job3 by joining it with the syslog_severity table, which is stored in Kudu and has the definition of each one of the severity levels.

  1. On the Explorer view, right-click on the Jobs item and select New Job to create a new job. Call it job4.

  2. Enter the following query in the SQL editor:

   SELECT
     a.window_start, a.window_end,
     a.severity,
     b.severity_desc,
     count(*) as severity_count
   FROM
     TABLE(
       HOP(TABLE syslog_data,
           DESCRIPTOR(event_time),
           INTERVAL '5' SECOND,
           INTERVAL '30' SECOND)) a
     JOIN `USERNAME-dh-kudu`.`default`.`default.syslog_severity` b
       ON a.severity = b.severity
   GROUP BY
     a.window_start, a.window_end, a.severity, b.severity_desc
  1. Click Execute and check the results to verify that everything works as expected.
  2. Once you're done, Stop your job.

docs.title: 8. Create a Production job sending data to Kafka
docs.text:
So far, the results of all the jobs that you created were displayed on the screen but not saved anywhere. When you run jobs in production you will want to send the results somewhere (Kafka, databases, Kudu, HDFS, S3, etc.) SSB makes it really easy to write data to different locations. All you have to do is to create a Virtual Table mapped to that location and then INSERT into that table the results of the query that you are running. You will practice this in this section by modifying job 4 to send its results to a Kafka topic.

You will start by creating a topic to store the results of your query and then modify job4 so that it sends its aggregated and enriched stream output to that topic.

  1. Open the Stream Messaging Manager (SMM) UI

  2. Click on the Topics icon and then on the Add New button to create a new topic

  3. Enter the following properties for your topic:

  4. Topic Name: USERNAME-severity-counts
  5. Partitions: 1
  6. Availability: MAXIMUM
  7. Cleanup Policy: delete

  1. Back in the SSB UI, select job4 in the Explorer pane to open the SQL editor for it. You should see the aggregation query that you had created in the previous section.

  2. Before you can run this job in production you need to create a Virtual Table in SSB and map it to the USERNAME-severity-counts Kafka topic that was created above.

The structure/schema of this table must match the structure of the output of the query that is being executed. Thankfully, SSB has a template feature that makes this very easy to do.

Click on the Templates button above the SQL editor and select upsert-kafka > json.

You will notice that a CREATE TABLE template was inserted at the beginning of the editor. Scroll up and down to check the contents of the editor. Please do NOT execute it yet.

  1. The added template is a CREATE TABLE statement to create a Virtual Table of the type you selected. Before you can execute it you have to complete the template with the missing information.

Make the following changes to the template: 1. Table name: change the table name to USERNAME_severity_counts 2. Primary key: add the following primary key clause after the last column in the table (severity_count): 

PRIMARY KEY (`window_start`, `window_end`, `severity`) NOT ENFORCED

  1. Fill in the properties in the WITH clause(we will copy kafka brokers from the SMM Datahub page):
'connector' = 'upsert-kafka',
'key.format' = 'json',
'properties.bootstrap.servers' = '<broker1>:9093,<broker2>:9093,<broker3>:9093',
'topic' = 'USERNAME-severity-counts',
'value.format' = 'json'

There are other optional properties commented out in the template that you can ignore. The completed template should look like the one below:

  1. With your mouse, select only the text of the entire CREATE TABLE statement and click on the Execute Selection button to run only that statement and create the Virtual Table.

After the CREATE TABLE execution you can see the created table in the Explorer tree:

  1. Once the table is created successfully, delete the CREATE TABLE statement from the SQL editor.

  2. Modify the original query in the editor by adding the following line before the SELECT keyword: 

       INSERT INTO `USERNAME_severity_counts`

Your final statement should look like this:

  1. Select the section of the query you want to execute and click on the Execute button to submit your job for execution.

  2. You should see the output of the query on the Results tab once the job starts executing. You can close the tab or window at any time and the job will continue running on the Flink cluster.

  3. Open the SMM UI again, click on the Topics icon and search for the USERNAME-severity-counts topic.

  4. Click on the Data Explorer icon () for the topic to visualize the data in the topic. You should be able to see recently added data with the aggregations produced by job4:

docs.title: 9. Troubleshooting Flink/SSB jobs
docs.text:
If you have problems with running your jobs, follow the steps below to check job details in SSB and on the Flink Dashboard.

  1. Click on your job (under Jobs on the left bar) to open the job editor:

  1. Click on the Flink Dashboard link to open the Flink Dashboard for job

  1. Navigate the dashboard pages to explore details and metrics of the job execution:

  1. Browse the job's DAG. Click on each of the operators (blue boxes) to see metrics and details of each one, including their individual tasks.

We have now concluded Lab 2

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
Cloudera provides Kafka Connect connectors that use Debezium libraries to provide Change Data Capture (CDC) functionality. This makes it very simple to capture transactional data from the most common databases (Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL) and process that data in a streaming data in real time.

Debezium provides a unified format schema for changelog and supports serialization of messages using JSON and Apache Avro. This can enable a number of use cases, including:

  • Synchronizing incremental data from databases to other systems
  • Collecting and storing audit records from database changes

In this module you will configure and use Kafka Connect to capture changes being made to a PostgreSQL database.

docs.title: 2. Required details
docs.text:
The PostgreSQL database used in the workshop is hosted in a VM created in the cloud environment. To connect to PostgreSQL you must first connect to the VM (using your web browser) and then connect to PostgreSQL using the command line tool psql.

Your workshop instructor will share the IP address and credentials to connect to the VM and to the PostgreSQL database. Before starting the workshop, ensure you have the following details for your group:

Credential Value 🖥️ VM IP Address ec2-18-218-191-235.us-east-2.compute.amazonaws.com 👤 OS Username workshop 🔑 OS Password cloudera 🗄️ DB Host IP localhost 🧑‍💻 DB Username cdc_USERNAME 🔐 DB Password cloudera 💾 DB Name DB_NAME

docs.title: 3. Create a work table in the PostgreSQL database
docs.text:
1. Open a new browser tab and connect to https://ec2-18-218-191-235.us-east-2.compute.amazonaws.com/workshop/
  2. Login with the OS credentials listed in the table above
  3. Once you are logged in, execute the following command to connect to your assigned PostgreSQL database: 
       psql --host localhost --port 5432 --user cdc_USERNAME --dbname DB_NAME

The username and database name will be automatically populated based on your input at the top of the page.

docs.title: 🐘 Quick PSQL Cheat Sheet
4. Deploy the PostgresConnector
docs.text:
You will now deploy a PostgresConnector in Kafka Connect to capture changes in your assigned database.

  1. In the CDP Console, find the Streams Messaging (Kafka) DataHub of your environment and click on it to open the DataHub page.
  2. Click on the
  3. icon to open the SMM UI
  4. In the SMM UI, click on the Connect icon () on the left-side bar to open the Kafka Connect page.
  5. Click on the New Connector button to add a new connector.
  6. In the Select A Template page, click on the Source Template PostgresConnector.
  7. Once the property fields for the PostgresConnector appear, enter a name for your connector in the first field at the top. Call it: test-cdc-USERNAME
  8. Set the properties for the connector as per the table below:
connector.class io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector database.dbname DB_NAME database.hostname ec2-18-218-191-235.us-east-2.compute.amazonaws.com database.password cloudera database.port 5432 database.user cdc_USERNAME plugin.name pgoutput tasks.max 3 topic.prefix pg_USERNAME

Important: The property database.server.name is not the hostname of the PostgreSQL server. This property is an arbitrary string that will be used to prefix the name of the topics created by this connector. The connector will create one topic per table in the specified database.

  1. There are additional properties needed to complete the connector configuration. Add the properties below by clicking on the icons in the page:
Property Value database.server.name pg_USERNAME producer.override.sasl.mechanism PLAIN producer.override.security.protocol SASL_SSL slot.name debezium_pg_USERNAME publication.autocreate.mode all_tables schema.include.list public snapshot.mode initial producer.override.sasl.jaas.config org.apache.kafka.common.security.plain.PlainLoginModule required username="USERNAME" password="WORKLOAD_PASSWORD";

Important: CDP Workload Password Required

For the producer.override.sasl.jaas.config property, you MUST use your CDP Workload Password.

The format of input value should be: 

org.apache.kafka.common.security.plain.PlainLoginModule required username="USERNAME" password="<YOUR_WORKLOAD_PASSWORD>";

Example (using user001 with workload password user001SecretPassword): 

org.apache.kafka.common.security.plain.PlainLoginModule required username="user001" password="user001SecretPassword";

Example of a completed PostgresConnector configuration form:

  1. Once you have entered all the properties above, click on the Validate button. If the validation succeeds you will see the following message:

Otherwise, fix the errors and try validating again until all the errors are fixed.

  1. Click the Next button (at the bottom) to continue.

  2. Review the information in the Configuration Review page and if everything is correct click Deploy to deploy the connector. If the deployment is successful you will see the following message:

  3. Click on the View Connector Profile button to see the connector details. You should see the connector status as RUNNING, with a green status icon:

docs.title: 5. Generate database activity
docs.text:
1. If you are not connected to the PostgreSQL database, connect to it using psql (see steps 3.1 to 3.3 above)
  2. Execute the following commands below to generate activity on the work table 
       INSERT INTO worktable VALUES (1, 'ONE');

   INSERT INTO worktable VALUES (2, 'TWO');

   INSERT INTO worktable VALUES (3, 'THREE');

   UPDATE worktable SET col2 = 'TROIS' WHERE col1 = 3;

   DELETE FROM worktable WHERE col1 = 2;

   SELECT * FROM worktable;

docs.title: 6. Verify results
docs.text:
1. In the SMM UI, click on the Connect icon () on the left-side bar to open the Kafka Connect page.

  2. Find your deployed connector (test-cdc-USERNAME) and click on it. The UI will show arrows from the connector to the associated topic(s), similar to the picture below:

  3. Click on the icon of the associated topic. The topic metrics page will open.

  4. Click on the DATA EXPLORER tab and browse through the data generated by the PostgresConnector.

Each message corresponds to one database transaction. You should be able to identify the following transactions, which correspond to the database changes performed previously.

We have now concluded Lab 4
